info.text: Western meter is two questions at once: how many beats fill a bar, and whether each of those beats splits in two or in three.

clusters.name: Beat grouping
clusters.fact: Duple, triple, and quadruple meter classify how many counting-pulse beats occupy a bar: two, three, or four — the slower pulse layer, not how each beat subdivides.

duple meter.text: Two counting-pulse beats in each bar — a march, a polka, or a fast 6/8.

quadruple meter.text: Four counting-pulse beats in each bar. Some theorists treat it as two duple groups, but it is the usual pulse of pop and rock, with its own four-beat accent pattern.

triple meter.text: Three counting-pulse beats in each bar — the waltz, the minuet, the mazurka.

info.text: How many beats occupy a bar.

clusters.name: Beat division
clusters.fact: Simple meter divides each beat into two equal parts; compound meter divides each beat into three, so the beat itself is written as a dotted note.

compound meter.text: Each beat divides into three equal parts. The top number is 6, 9, or 12, and the bottom number names one division of the beat, not the beat.

dotted beat.text: In compound meter the beat is always a dotted note — three times as long as the division. In 6/8 that beat is a dotted quarter.

simple meter.text: Each beat divides into two equal parts. The top number of the time signature is 2, 3, or 4, and the bottom number names the beat itself.

info.text: Whether each beat splits in two or in three.

bridges.fact: 4/4 is simple quadruple meter: four beats to the bar, each dividing in two — the most common written meter in popular and classical music.

info.text: Four quarter-note beats, each splitting into two eighths. Also written as common time (C).

bridges.fact: 3/4 is simple triple meter: three beats to the bar, each dividing in two. A waltz is counted in three, not as one compound beat.

info.text: Three quarter-note beats, each splitting into two eighths — six eighths on the page, counted in three.

bridges.fact: 6/8 is compound duple meter: two dotted-quarter beats to the bar, each dividing into three eighths. The same six eighth notes as 3/4, grouped as two beats rather than three.

info.text: Two dotted-quarter beats, each splitting into three eighths — six eighths on the page, counted in two.

lenses.prompt: Which terms name how many beats occupy a bar, rather than how a beat splits or a written time signature?
lenses.explanation: These three names are grouping sizes, not written meters and not ways a beat splits. 4/4 has four beats, but it is a signature, not the name of the four-beat grouping.

reasons.duple meter: The name for two beats to the bar.
reasons.quadruple meter: The name for four beats to the bar.
reasons.triple meter: The name for three beats to the bar.

lenses.explanation: Both signatures show six eighth notes. 6/8 counts them as two dotted beats (compound duple); 3/4 counts them as three undotted beats (simple triple).

reasons.compound meter: 6/8 divides each beat in three; 3/4 divides each beat in two.
reasons.dotted beat: The 6/8 beat is a dotted quarter; 3/4 beats are undotted quarters.
reasons.duple meter: 6/8 has two beats to the bar; 3/4 has three.
